and wide’ (l. 38), and among the cancellations in the draft there lies ‘a thread of moon-light’
(see note to l. 46). All these conditions are best met on the night of 22 or 23 June: according
to Mary ‘The heats set in in the middle of June; the days became excessively hot’ (‘Note on
Poems of 1822’, 1839 iv 231); for 22 June Williams recorded in his journal: ‘Calm. Heat
overpowering’ (Gisborne Jnl 155). There was a new moon on the morning of 19 June; on
22 and 23 the moon reached its meridian in the late afternoon and set from two to three
hours after the sun had set at 19:46. On 23 June, at least, it would have been bright enough
to give some moonlight but still narrow enough to be compared to a hovering albatross.
